episode_title: Inside the Hearts of Men and Women

stories.summary: Many years ago Amit wrote a column arguing that India's rising divorce rates were a damn good thing — because they signal women's empowerment, more women gaining the agency to leave bad marriages. The piece was controversial at the time but is the seed of an entire frame for measuring empowerment through unconventional metrics.
stories.insight: What looks like social decay can be moral progress in disguise. The 'rising rate of X' is meaningless without asking who used to be trapped in non-X — divorce rates, women in prisons, solo women travelers — all flip from 'bad' to 'good' once you put agency at the center.

stories.topic: Hamsini Hariharan's 'More Women in Prisons' Metric
stories.summary: On the Seen and Unseen episode 'Metrics of Empowerment,' Hamsini Hariharan proposed that more women in prisons is a fantastic metric of women's empowerment — it means more women have agency, more opportunity to commit crime, more presence in public life beyond the home. Nidhi Gupta added: look at how many families a 'large child' (eldest) is male, as a proxy for sex-selective stopping rules.
stories.insight: The most revealing metrics are the ones you'd never put on a dashboard. Empowerment is about exposure to the full set of human experiences — including the bad ones — not about being shielded from the world.

stories.topic: The Pizza Decision-Tree Test for Agency
stories.summary: In the Life Lessons course, Ajay distinguishes who really has agency in a household by walking through the pizza order: who decides 'let's have pizza,' who decides 'let's order Domino's,' and who finally taps the app. If the menfolk decide the first two and instruct the woman to 'just order it,' the fact that her phone placed the order tells you nothing about her agency.
stories.insight: Surface-level digital traces (who tapped 'order') can completely hide the upstream power structure. To measure agency you have to disentangle the decision tree, not just count taps.

stories.topic: The Air-Conditioner That Was Designed for Men in Suits
stories.summary: When air conditioning entered offices in the 1950s and 60s, default temperatures were calibrated for men in suits, ignoring that women have different metabolic rates. The result is the eternal married-couple argument — 'I'm cold' / 'put on a sweater' — and a default that quietly imposes a male body norm on shared workspaces. Ajay proposes the office AC default temperature as a slow-moving metric of gender equilibrium.
stories.insight: Infrastructure carries a frozen anthropology. The temperature on the wall is not a neutral fact; it's a 70-year-old cultural assumption about whose body the room is designed for.

stories.summary: Ajay proposes a small project anyone can build today: stick a tele-lens camera outside a window pointed at a stretch of pavement, run modern image classifiers to count people and infer gender, and you immediately get two things — the female fraction of public-square users, and the way that fraction collapses as evening falls. He links this to crime-victimisation surveys where parents are asked what time their teenage daughter is allowed to be out.
stories.insight: The presence of women in public space at night is one of the cleanest scalar measures of how free a society actually is. With cheap cameras and open-source vision models, this is a measurement waiting to be built.

stories.topic: The 'Is Immoral to Have Children' Column and Why Parents Got Furious
stories.summary: Amit once wrote, partly to provoke, that it is immoral to have children — and parents got really pissed off. After reading Stephens-Davidowitz's data he finally understood why: people are seven times more likely to ask Google whether they will regret not having children than whether they will regret having them, but adults with children are 3.6 times more likely to tell Google they regret the decision than adults without. The reaction wasn't to the argument; it was to a hidden private regret being touched.
stories.insight: The strength of a backlash is often a clue to a hidden truth, not a hidden lie. Parenthood is durable, irreversible, and (for many) regretted in private — which is why public questioning of it draws disproportionate fury.

stories.summary: Twenty-five years ago Amit went down what would today be called the manosphere rabbit hole, fascinated by it as a window into human nature. He read Neil Strauss's The Game — a bestseller marketed as a pickup-artist handbook but which, beneath the manipulation, displayed a sharp understanding of how desire and validation work. That ecosystem has since metastasised into the Andrew Tate / Gumroad / Adolescence world.
stories.insight: Subcultures that society dismisses as creepy or fringe are often the first to articulate something real about a system's failure modes. Reading them seriously — without endorsing them — is part of how you map the social terrain.

stories.summary: Malini Goyal's book Unboxing Bengaluru measured how long it takes someone meeting on Tinder to end up at the other person's house in three Indian cities. Delhi: months. Mumbai: weeks. Bangalore: days. Causes are layered — Delhi is a low-trust society, Mumbai housing is a premium and people live with families, Bangalore singles tend to live alone — but the qualitative work that followed showed the punchline: among the apps' heavy users, promiscuity was off the charts and nobody was happy.
stories.insight: Frictionless matching plus low frictional cost of switching produces high-volume, low-investment encounters. With ten alternatives chatting in real time, no one puts in the work to repair a small fight — and a real relationship is mostly the work of repairing small fights.

stories.topic: The Parade's End Quote on Why You Have to Live With Someone
stories.summary: Ajay reads a passage from Ford Madox Ford's Parade's End: 'You seduced a young woman in order to be able to finish your talks with her... You may not be in the mood when she is in the mood for the intimate conversation that means the final communion of your souls. You have to wait together for a week, for a year, for a lifetime, before the final intimate conversation may be attained.' His point: the reason couples cohabit isn't what people pretend; it's that the deepest conversation can only be reached by waiting through all the moods.
stories.insight: Long companionship is a search algorithm for a vanishingly rare moment of genuine communion — and that moment can't be scheduled, only waited into. Dating-app speed is precisely the wrong shape of time for finding it.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Wouldn't Date Within Her College
stories.summary: Amit recalls a quote from a survey: a young woman explained she went on dating apps rather than dating someone from her college because if it didn't work out she'd have to see him every day — and worse, see him with another girl every day. The dating app is, among other things, an instrument for the geographic disposability of failed relationships.
stories.insight: Dating apps don't just expand the pool — they offer a pre-built escape route. The willingness to date is partly a function of how cleanly you can exit, and modern matching is engineered to make exit nearly costless.

stories.topic: Setting the VPN to Australia and Reading Search Autocompletes
stories.summary: Amit ran the Stephens-Davidowitz experiment himself — Google autocomplete in incognito, with ExpressVPN switched between locations. India's top 'my husband wants me to' completions today include 'serve his mistress' and (until recently) 'breastfeed his friends.' Australia's top completions include 'open marriage,' 'second wife,' and 'eat my poop.' The cultural fingerprint of a country sits naked in its searchbar.
stories.insight: The Google searchbar is the closest instrument we have to a global, anonymous, polygraph-grade window into private mental life. Ten minutes with autocomplete tells you more about a country than a week of polite interviews.

stories.topic: The Bus Full of Men Who Want to Be Breastfed
stories.summary: After reading the Indian search data, Amit jokes that next time he's in a bus he'll look around and think, '30% of these men want to be breastfed, what the fuck, dude' — judging every guy in sight. Ajay's serious counter is that the analogy breaks down because Amit's social bubble is unrepresentative; the searches reflect the median Indian, who lives a very different life.
stories.insight: Anonymous-aggregate data forces you to confront that the median person is not a person you know. That confrontation is a corrective to elite empathy gaps — but only if you remember that the data describes society, not the next person you meet.

recommendations.item: Everybody Lies
recommendations.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
recommendations.context: The book at the heart of Chapter 2, on what anonymised Google search data reveals about the human condition.
recommendations.reason: The seminal popular text on the idea that people are most truly themselves when searching anonymously online — turning the searchbar into a polygraph for the secret self. Source of the book's most-cited findings, from sexless marriages to gender-biased parenting Google queries.

recommendations.item: The Truth About Ourselves
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's essay for Pragati on Everybody Lies.
recommendations.reason: His own working-out of why search data matters more than survey data — and a useful entry point to the chapter's argument.

recommendations.item: Polls Get Elections Wrong. So Use Google
recommendations.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
recommendations.context: Stephens-Davidowitz's column showing that in states where people searched for 'Trump-Harris debate' Trump won, and in states searching 'Harris-Trump debate' Harris won.
recommendations.reason: A vivid demonstration that word order in search queries beat televised polling. The kind of finding only an algorithm would surface, and once surfaced, never quite leaves you.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's controversial column reframing rising divorce rates as a sign of women's empowerment.
recommendations.reason: The seed of the entire 'unconventional metrics of empowerment' frame that opens the episode.

recommendations.item: It Is Immoral to Have Children. Here's Why
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's deliberately provocative antinatalism column.
recommendations.reason: Returned to here in light of Stephens-Davidowitz's finding that adults with children are 3.6x more likely to Google their regret than adults without — explaining why the column drew such ferocious personal hostility.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ashwini Deshpande
recommendations.context: Deshpande's labour economics on gender and caste.
recommendations.reason: Companion reading for the FLFP puzzle and broader empirical work on Indian women's economic lives.

recommendations.item: Crime Victimisation in India
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and co-editors
recommendations.context: An edited volume in the field Ajay has worked in.

recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: trends.google.com — fixed-query strings you can run to watch the world's attention move in real time.

recommendations.item: Adolescence
recommendations.creator: Jack Thorne and Stephen Graham
recommendations.context: The Netflix limited series dramatising how the manosphere reaches a teenage boy.
recommendations.reason: A small-window dramatisation of why incel grievances don't come from nowhere — they refract real Tinder-Gini-coefficient data through a young man's life. (The episode notes the show captures only a sliver of the broader manosphere ecosystem.)

recommendations.item: The Game
recommendations.creator: Neil Strauss
recommendations.context: The 2005 pickup-artist memoir/handbook that catalysed an entire ecosystem.
recommendations.reason: A bestseller that, beneath the manipulation, displayed a sharp folk understanding of human nature. Worth reading both as anthropology of the manosphere and as a lens on how validation economies work.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier episode on Rob Henderson's 'luxury beliefs' frame.

recommendations.item: Rob Henderson's tweet on dark-triad men and the dating-app defect-defect equilibrium
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Henderson's long Twitter thread on how psychopathic men, exploited women, and ordinary men drive each other into mutual mistreatment on dating apps.
recommendations.reason: The single most-quoted text in Chapter 3 — Amit reads it out in full as the core explanation of why dating-app dynamics generate so much bitterness on every side.

recommendations.creator: Soulmatcher (2025)
recommendations.context: A 2025 industry report on declining trust and rising pessimism among singles.
recommendations.reason: Quantitative backing for Henderson's qualitative thesis: women losing trust in strangers, men feeling unfairly excluded, both opting out.

recommendations.item: When Harry Met Sally
recommendations.creator: Rob Reiner
recommendations.context: Nora Ephron and Rob Reiner's 1989 film with Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan, including the Katz's Deli scene Amit calls 'the greatest orgasm in movie history.'

recommendations.item: The Facebook Study on Cross-Gender Social Ties
recommendations.creator: Facebook research
recommendations.context: Study mapping 1.4 trillion links among 1.8 billion adult Facebook users, estimating closeness of each connection and producing a per-region cross-gender friendship index.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pick for measurement enthusiasts: micro-level data down to the lowest GADM administrative units, suitable as a staple variable for researchers studying the gender geography of any city or district.

recommendations.item: Can Men and Women Be Just Friends?
recommendations.creator: The Economist
recommendations.context: The Economist's piece naming the Facebook cross-gender index after When Harry Met Sally.
recommendations.reason: Where the 'WIMSY' framing is laid out — including India's surprisingly high score of 0.35.

recommendations.item: Parade's End
recommendations.creator: Ford Madox Ford
recommendations.context: Ford Madox Ford's tetralogy.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's read-aloud passage on why long companionship is necessary to ever finish a real conversation — the romantic counterweight to the chapter's data on app-driven disposability.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal quoting Christ Williamson on hiding your true self
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: A short piece on the cost of inauthenticity — if you don't reveal your true self, you can't be loved for who you are.
recommendations.reason: Amit cites this idea (also attributed to Paul Graham) to bridge from search-data inauthenticity to the deeper cost of self-suppression.

recommendations.item: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Episode 116 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on satellite-based measurement.
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the contrasting case to dating-app data: bird-in-the-sky measurement leaves North Korea unaffected, whereas dating apps simultaneously measure and transform the system.

recommendations.item: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us (Episode 117 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE measurement episode.
recommendations.reason: Direct setup for this episode — episode 117 was so loaded with measurement findings that the men-and-women material was carved off into a separate show.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit and Ajay's online course at lifelessons.co.in.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pizza-decision-tree example for parsing agency comes directly from the Life Lessons curriculum.

core_ideas.explanation: Standard empowerment metrics (literacy, FLFP) miss the texture of agency. Unconventional ones reveal more: rising divorce rates, solo women travellers, the share of families whose eldest child is male, the number of women in prisons, men downloading grocery apps, default office AC temperatures, the female share of pavement traffic at 9pm. The pattern is that you measure agency by exposure to the full set of human possibilities — including failure, conflict, and crime — not by protection from them.
core_ideas.quote: Rising divorce rates are a sign of women's empowerment. It means more and more women are getting the agency to leave bad marriages.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Selves and the Searchbar as Polygraph
core_ideas.explanation: Borrowing from Garcia Marquez: the public self (known to all), the private self (known to a Dunbar-tiny inner circle), and the secret self (known to no one). Stephens-Davidowitz's insight is that when we search anonymously online, we behave as if no one is watching — so the secret self leaks. The searchbar becomes the only mass-scale instrument that captures it. 'Facebook is digital brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum'; Google is the opposite.
core_ideas.quote: Garcia Marquez often talks about how we have three selves: the public self, the private self, and the secret self.

core_ideas.concept: Stated Preferences vs Revealed Preferences vs Search Preferences
core_ideas.explanation: Economists already distinguish what people say (stated) from what they do (revealed). Search data introduces a third, even more honest layer: what people privately wonder. Only 25% of women admit in surveys to searching for porn; the actual number is far higher. Men make as many searches for how to perform oral sex on themselves as for how to give a woman an orgasm. These wonderings are not actions but they are not lies either — they reveal the architecture of private desire.

Run Google autocomplete on 'my husband wants me to' from different VPN locations and you get a country's secret cultural fingerprint. India today: 'serve his mistress'; recently 'breastfeed his friends.' Australia: 'open marriage,' 'second wife,' 'eat my poop.' Indian porn searches for women breastfeeding men are 4x higher than any other country. The interpretive challenge is real (why? what cultural mechanism?) but the data is unmistakeable: each society sublimates its repressions into a unique pattern of search.

core_ideas.concept: The Gender Bias of Parents, Algorithmically Exposed
core_ideas.explanation: Parents are 2.5x more likely to ask 'is my son gifted' than 'is my daughter gifted,' and 2x more likely to ask 'is my daughter overweight' than 'is my son overweight' — even though girls have larger vocabularies, are more likely to enter gifted programs, and 35% of boys vs 20% of girls are actually overweight. The bias is global; in India it is almost certainly worse. A bias too embarrassing to admit on a survey is exposed in a thousand small searches.

Across the Tinder population, men face a 0.58 Gini coefficient on female attention — more unequal than 95% of countries' income distributions. Women swipe right on 5-14% of profiles; men swipe right on roughly 50%. Men are 6.2x more likely to like a given woman than vice versa. The result is a small fraction of attractive men collecting most of the female attention while the median man gets nothing — generating real bitterness, the modern incel population, and the manosphere ecosystem.
core_ideas.quote: Women hold all the cards. Men are 6.2 times more likely to like a woman than vice versa.

core_ideas.concept: Communities of Circumstance vs Communities of Choice
core_ideas.explanation: Pre-internet life was a community of circumstance — geography and social caste fixed who you could meet, befriend, marry. The internet enabled communities of choice, where weirdos and minorities and the lonely can find each other. This is unambiguously good for LGBTQ people (a gay man born in 1960 could spend his whole life alone; one born in 2000 cannot). It also restructures romance: 60% of recent marriages start online. Most of Amit's friends today are people he met online.

core_ideas.concept: Selectivity Explosion: Hardware Is Old, Choice Set Is New
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's response to the question 'what's actually changed since the dawn of modern man?' Hardwired desire (men: youth/beauty; women: status/affluence — biologists' framing, not endorsed normatively) has been stable for tens of thousands of years. What's new is that the choice set went from ~10 men/10 women (pre-internet circle) to ~1 million in your pocket (dating apps). Selection becomes ruthless; the top of the distribution is winner-take-all. Same instincts, drastically different equilibrium because the matching surface exploded.
core_ideas.quote: The instincts were always the same because they are what they are, but the behaviours have changed.

core_ideas.concept: Heisenberg Measurement: Dating Apps Both Reveal and Transform
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: nighttime-lights satellite imagery reveals North Korea without affecting it. Dating-app data is the opposite — the act of measurement (the existence of dating apps) is itself the cause of the new behaviours being measured. You can't run the counterfactual; the instrument has rewritten the system. Any social-data tool that makes a behaviour newly observable should be presumed to also be reshaping that behaviour.
core_ideas.quote: On one hand the phenomena are rendered observable by the dating apps. But the dating apps have completely changed the system as well.

core_ideas.explanation: Rob Henderson's model of the dating-app social system: dark-triad men (psychopathy, narcissism, Machiavellianism) make up 10-20% of users but are excellent imposters who collect disproportionate sex partners while damaging the women they sleep with. Those women, traumatised, become wary and begin to behave in psychopathic and narcissistic ways themselves to even the score, especially against ordinary men. Those men become resentful and treat ordinary women the same way. Bad behavior drives out the good; the equilibrium is universal cold cynicism even though almost no one wanted it.
core_ideas.quote: Bad behaviour drives out the good. A system tailor-made for psychopathic males predictably gives rise to a defect-defect equilibrium.

core_ideas.explanation: Despite (or because of) frictionless matching, Gen Z is having less sex than millennials. Three out of ten men in surveys report no sex in the last year; one in four women say the same. The Romantic Recession Report finds women avoiding strangers, men feeling 'women don't give us a fair chance.' The system that promised infinite romantic abundance has produced widespread voluntary opt-out — many young people are turning back toward family-formation values.

core_ideas.concept: Marriage as a Bundled Equilibrium That No Longer Holds
core_ideas.explanation: Marriage evolved as an uneasy equilibrium when you knew few people and social norms were enforced — bundling love, sex, companionship, friendship, parenting into one institution that left both parties mildly satisfied / mildly unsatisfied but stable. When the choice set explodes and the social-norm enforcement weakens, the bundle starts to fall apart. The unbundling raises questions modern society has not solved: how do you organize relationships when each component can be obtained separately, with different partners, at different times?

core_ideas.concept: The When Harry Met Sally Index (WIMSY)
core_ideas.explanation: Facebook mapped 1.4 trillion social ties among 1.8 billion adults and produced a cross-gender friendship index, where 0 = total gender segregation and 1 = equal cross-gender and same-gender friend counts. The Economist proposed naming it after the Billy Crystal/Meg Ryan film whose premise is that men and women can't be just friends. India scores 0.35 — surprisingly high, given the social repression and male inability to talk to women. The data is broken out at sub-district resolution, making it a powerful new variable for measuring the social geography of gender.

Amit's bridge from search-data findings to ethics: if we are not our authentic selves in public, we cannot be truly loved — because no one can love what they have not been allowed to see. Stephens-Davidowitz finds many of us aren't even authentic to ourselves; we deny in our own minds what our searches expose. The cost of this hiddenness isn't just statistical bias in surveys — it's the foreclosure of intimacy.

core_ideas.concept: Economists Are Working on the Wrong Problem
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's closing argument: technocratic public-policy economics — GDP-by-half-percent, inflation targeting — is essentially a lost game in India and not where the deep questions live. The deeper questions are about society itself: communication between humans, the impossibility of fully knowing another person, the gendered fissures revealed by data like this. A good economist's frameworks (psychology, sociology, anthropology, genetics, literature) should be redirected at the great mystery of humanity, not at marginal macro tweaks that won't be implemented anyway.
core_ideas.quote: It is impossible for any one person to communicate himself to another person. We can never truly know another person — and at one level, we can never truly know ourselves.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening line about Ajay: 'In this team the internal name for Amit Varma is the Energizer Bunny, because he goes on and on.' Cold open: 'We were joking earlier about how Ajay Shah comes in five seconds.'
Ajay on the phrase 'digital exhaust': 'Digital exhaust — which is basically a phone running out of battery.'

Amit on porn-vs-weather searches: 'In fact, many more men search for porn than for weather — except you, I think you search a lot for weather. But you can't jerk off to clouds. So there's an understandable reason for that.'

Amit on judging strangers post-search-data: 'Next time I'm in a bus, I will look around and I will think, huh, 30% of these men want to be breastfed, what the fuck, dude. I'll be like judging every guy out there.'

Amit on the Australian autocomplete result 'my husband wants to eat my poop': 'I can only gather that Australians want to read books about the things that they are bothered about, because [their top result is] an open marriage novel.'

Stephens-Davidowitz on female anxieties about vaginal smell — fish, vinegar, onions, ammonia, garlic, cheese, body odor, urine, bread, bleach, feces, sweat, metal, feet, garbage, rotten meat: 'We are all so busy judging our own bodies that there is little energy left over to judge other people.'

Amit on what oral-self-search reveals: 'Men make as many searches looking for ways to perform oral sex on themselves as they do how to give women an orgasm.' Two deep truths about men: self-obsession and stupidity.
Ajay on Ajay's cooperation with Tinder: 'Have you ever been on a dating app, Ajay?' / 'For about ten seconds.' / 'You lasted twice as long as one would expect. Well done.'
Amit, after Ajay reads the Parade's End passage in about fifteen seconds: 'If you add it to your act, you can last twenty seconds. And she'll also come when she hears you.'

Amit on the WIMSY index name: 'I was calling it the WIMSY index till I realized that the I at the end of it stands for index. So it would be like calling it When Harry Met Sally Index Index, which we don't want to do.'
Amit on swiping right on Ajay: 'I would always swipe right on you. But anyway, if swipe right is the correct direction.'
'Dance like no one's looking' — Amit's reframe of search behaviour: when we search online, we are expressing ourselves as if no one's looking.
Gabriel Garcia Marquez's three selves: public, private, secret. Used as the architecture for why search data is uniquely valuable — it captures the secret self that survives no other instrument.
When Harry Met Sally (Rob Reiner, 1989) — the Katz's Deli orgasm scene; Billy Crystal's premise that men and women can't be friends 'because the sex part always gets in the way.'

Ford Madox Ford, Parade's End: 'You seduced a young woman in order to be able to finish your talks with her... You have to wait together for a week, for a year, for a lifetime, before the final intimate conversation may be attained and exhausted.'

Georges Simenon's lifelong theme that 'it is impossible for any one person to communicate himself to another person' — Ajay's lodestar for what literature has been trying to teach us, and what economists should be willing to take seriously.
'Hamara dil sagar ki tarah' / 'Our heart is like an ocean, mysterious and...' — episode closer, gesturing at the inexhaustibility of what data and literature alike are trying to map.
'A long, long time ago, I can still remember' — Amit echoing Don McLean's American Pie in introducing the Metrics of Empowerment episode.
Rob Henderson's coinage 'luxury beliefs' and his dark-triad / defect-defect dating-app thread — quoted at length as the chapter's load-bearing diagnosis.
Neil Strauss's The Game (2005) and the modern Gumroad-and-TikTok manosphere it spawned — name-checked as the lineage running through Andrew Tate-style content and the show Adolescence.
